Any of these modalities are appropriate for women 30 to 39 years. C

Clinically suspicious masses should be biopsied despite negative imaging results. C

background.definition: A breast lump is a discrete mass of breast tissue that is different in size, shape, and texture from surrounding breast tissue and is different from the contralateral breast.

list.listitem: In a study in an American health maintenance organization, there were 8.3 presentations per year for breast mass evaluation per 1000 women between the ages of 40 and 69 years.
Breast cancer prevalence in women with a breast lump increases with age: 1% in women younger than 40 years, 9% in women between the ages of 41 and 55 years, and 37% in women older than 55 years.
Breast cancer makes up 29.7% of the cancers in females, making it the leading cause of cancer in women and the second leading cause of cancer death among women in the United States.

Among women with breast lumps, breast cancer was more likely to be detected in Asian/Pacific Islander women (84.2/1000 exams, 95% confidence interval (CI) 72.0-98.2) and Black women (81.4/1000 exams, 95% CI 69.4-95.2) based on 51,014 diagnostic mammograms performed between 2005 and 2018 in the Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium. The lowest cancer rates were among Hispanic/Latina women (42.9/1000 exams, 95% CI 34.2-53.6).

In a population-based mammography screening study in Finland, breast cancer detection rates were 4.7 per 1,000 screening visits for women without symptoms, 7.8 per 1,000 for women with symptoms, and 32 per 1,000 screens for women with a breast lump. The odds ratio of breast cancer among women with a breast lump vs. no symptoms was 6.47 (95% CI 5.89-7.09).
Male breast cancer peaks at age 71 years and often presents as a breast lump. More than 40% of these men will present with stage III or stage IV disease.
Total cancer cost in the United States in 2015 was $183 billion; 20% to 25% of that cost was attributable to breast cancer.
Delayed diagnosis of breast cancer is the most common cause of malpractice in the United States.
The finding and evaluation of breast lumps causes significant psychological stress for patients.

listitem.strong: Future breast cancer in patients with prior breast lumps or benign breast disease

list.listitem: The relative risk (RR) of future breast cancer for the main categories of breast lesions, listed below, are: non-proliferative (RR 1.17, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.94-1.47), proliferative without atypia (RR 1.76, 95% CI 1.58-1.95), and atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia (RR 3.93, 95% CI 3.24-4.76). Lobular carcinoma in situ has the highest RR for future breast cancer of 6.8 to 11.

In a retrospective cohort study of 545,171 Spanish women aged 50-69 years screened biennially for breast cancer and followed for 6 years, the RR of breast cancer was 2.51 (95% CI 2.14-2.93) after a diagnosis of benign breast disease, RR 3.58 (95% CI 2.61-4.91) after a diagnosis of proliferative disease without atypia, and RR 4.56 (95% CI 2.06-10.07) after a diagnosis of proliferative disease with atypia.

In a Finnish population study, women with a breast lump had a hazard ratio of 3.7, 95% CI 3.0-4.6 for interval breast cancer and an increased fatal interval-cancer risk of 0.39 per 1000 screens. This same group of authors also found a significant difference in mortality rates, with 180 women with breast lumps per 10,000 person-years subsequently dying from breast cancer compared to 70 deaths per 10,000 person-years in those without a lump. All-cause mortality was also increased at 315 vs. 160 per 10,000 person-years in women with and without breast lumps, respectively.

The majority of breast lumps are due to benign causes. Categories of benign lesions include non-proliferative (simple cysts, mild hyperplasia, papillary apocrine change), proliferative without atypia (fibroadenoma, intraductal papilloma, moderate/florid hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis, radial scar), and atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia.
Simple cysts are a common benign cause, present in up to one third of women aged 35 to 50 years.
Fibroadenoma is also a common benign cause, particularly in adolescents and young adult women.

In a summary of 31 cases of unilateral breast enlargement in young males, ages 10-19 years, almost half (n=15) were considered idiopathic or familial gynecomastia with five patients diagnosed as secondary to androgen excess or treatment for various conditions, two with cystic lymphangioma, and one each for breast sarcoma and hematoma following trauma.
Lobular carcinoma in situ is not a cancer precursor but a risk factor for breast cancer. This lesion is multifocal in the ipsilateral breast and present in 30% of cases in the opposite breast.
Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common malignant cause.
Less common causes include infections, including tuberculosis.
The breast is made up of fat, glandular tissue, and various connective tissues.
Normal breasts have a heterogeneous texture.
The upper outer quadrant of the breast is the most nodular.
Breast texture changes in response to changing hormone levels.
Clinical breast examination B and self-breast examination A have not been shown to change mortality from breast cancer.
The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF, 2024) recommends biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 years.B
Regular screening with mammography and clinical breast examination will result in many false-positive results. B
Clinical breast examination and breast self-examination have not been shown to change mortality from breast cancer.
Current evidence does not demonstrate that breast cancer screening extends longevity.

The USPSTF (2024) guidelines give a Grade B recommendation for biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 years primarily to promote equity and not based on new evidence. For every 2000 women screened starting at age 40 years instead of 50 years, 3 more women avoid death and potentially gain 90 years of life at a cost of 1000 more false positives and 4 additional over-diagnosed cancers. Shared decision-making should be conducted for those 40-50 years.

The USPSTF 2024 concluded that current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of supplemental screening for breast cancer using breast ultrasonography or MRI in women identified to have dense breasts on an otherwise negative screening mammogram (I statement).

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG, 2021) provides a summary of guideline recommendations and considerations for breast cancer screening that can be used to involve patients in shared decision making. They recommend screening average risk women for breast cancer with mammography starting at age 40 years, initiating at no later than age 50 years, and screening every 1 to 2 years, with biennial screening mammography, particularly after age 55 years, as a reasonable option.

ACOG recommends that a risk assessment should be used for shared decision making for screening for breast cancer. A stepwise approach can be used. Step 1 is to take a thorough family history following either the USPSTF or NCCN approach. Step 2 is to ascertain personal history including risk factors and history of cancer. Step 3 is to select a risk prediction model; the three most commonly used models are the NCI Gail Model, the BCSC tool, and the IBIS/Tyrer-Cusick model. Step 4 is the interpretation of the risk assessment which aids in choosing a screening strategy and helps determine who is a candidate for risk reduction therapy.24

A retrospective cohort of 2400 women between the ages of 40 and 69 years found that over a 10-year period nearly 1 in 3 women had a false-positive screening result whereas only 1 in 27 women were actually diagnosed with breast cancer.

In the Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium database cited above, false-positive mammogram results per 1000 exams were most common among Asian/Pacific Islander women (183.9, 95% CI 126.7-259.2) and lowest among white women (112.4, 95% CI 86.1-145.5). After adjustment, false-positive as well as cancer detection rates remained higher for Asian/Pacific Islander and Black patients compared to their Hispanic/Latina and white counterparts.

Based on data from the Canadian National Breast Screening Study-I, for women ages 40 to 49 years, there was no effect of breast-cancer screening on breast-cancer mortality or all-cause mortality. Among regularly attending women, the cumulative risk of experiencing a false-positive test was 20.5%. Over-diagnosis of invasive breast cancer at 20 years post-cessation of screening was estimated to be 48%.

Both the United States Preventive Services Task Force and the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care recommend against routine teaching of breast self-examination. Women who find a breast lump incidentally should be encouraged to seek medical evaluation.

American College of Radiology guidelines (ACR, 2022) recommend ultrasound for women younger than 30 years and mammography or digital breast tomosynthesis diagnostic for women 40 years and older as the initial imaging modality for breast mass. Any of these modalities are appropriate for women 30 to 39 years. C

ACR (2022) recommends ultrasound for women age 40 years or older with a palpable mass and no definitive diagnosis following mammography or with suspicion of malignancy. For women under age 30 years with US findings suspicious for malignancy, mammography, digital breast tomosynthesis diagnostic or image-guided core biopsy are considered appropriate. C
Any breast lump brought to the attention of a clinician must be systematically evaluated. C

Because clinical examination is so poor at differentiating benign causes from malignant causes of breast lumps, aspiration or biopsy will often be required, based on the Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) assessment category using ultrasound, mammography or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Unilateral, soft, well circumscribed, usually round, sometimes ballotable (able to compress wall)
Involutional changes; may produce lumps, breast pain, nipple discharge, or retraction
Ill-defined, diffuse lumpiness, often tender, often in the upper outer quadrant, bilateral, changes with cycle
Irregular, firm, nontender, may be associated with trauma
Firm, mobile, located in axillary or supramammary area

list.listitem: Clinical breast examination has poor diagnostic accuracy. Therefore, aspiration or biopsy will almost always be needed to rule out malignancy when a woman presents with a breast lump.

Age, history of breast cancer in the patient or the patient's mother, mass size, mammography findings, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy results are useful in identifying breast cancer among women older than 30 years with a palpable breast lump.

In a retrospective study of 3,305 women age <40 years attending a one-stop breast clinic in the UK, 57.6% had a breast lump and breast cancer was diagnosed in 29 cases (0.88%). Although 27 of the 29 women diagnosed with cancer had a breast lump, only 6 of them had examination findings suspicious for cancer, 7 of 29 had ultrasound findings that were indeterminant or better, and 3 of 27 who underwent mammography had normal mammograms. Invasive ductal breast cancer was diagnosed on biopsy in 27, 1 woman had mixed ductal and lobular cancer and 1 had malignant melanoma. The investigators concluded that the triple test (evaluation by breast clinician, imaging evaluation, and fine needle aspiration or core biopsy) continues to be the recommended workup for breast lump even in relatively young women.

American College of Radiology guidelines (ACR, 2022) recommend ultrasound (US) for women younger than 30 years and mammography or digital breast tomosynthesis diagnostic for women 40 years and older as the initial imaging modality. Any of these modalities are appropriate for women 30 to 39 years.

ACR (2022) recommends US for women age 40 years or older with a palpable mass and no definitive diagnosis following mammography or with suspicion of malignancy. For women under age 30 years with US findings suspicious for malignancy, mammography, digital breast tomosynthesis diagnostic or image-guided core biopsy are recommended.
Mammography is useful to identify occult cancer in the rest of the ipsilateral breast and in the contralateral breast.
US is useful to differentiate solid masses from cystic masses, especially in younger women.

In a study of artificial intelligence (AI) software applied to breast US images compared to readings from a radiologist, AI correctly identified 47 or 48 of 49 women (96%-98%) with cancer with either portable US or standard of care US images, with areas under the curve of 0.91 and 0.95, respectively.

In one study, contrast-enhanced MRI for Category 3 calcified lesions had a sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV for malignancy of 84%, 82%, 58% and 95%, respectively. The use of non-invasive electrical impedance measurements and machine learning techniques is under investigation to potentially reduce biopsy rates.
Shear wave elastography may be useful for distinguishing between benign and malignant breast lesions (sensitivity 0.84-0.92 and specificity 0.87-0.89 for Asian and Caucasian women, respectively).

Fine-needle aspiration and core-needle biopsy have the advantage of being potentially therapeutic and potentially resulting in a cytologic diagnosis. The discriminative ability of a positive fine-needle aspiration for breast cancer is high (LR+ 44.5, LR− 0.11). A negative core biopsy is best for ruling out cancer (LR− 0.01).
Imaging modalities used for guidance, such as ultrasound, may improve the accuracy of fine-needle aspiration and core-needle biopsy results.

In a 7-year retrospective study of 166 patients with suspicious clinical breast findings and normal imaging who underwent a clinical core biopsy and 117 similar cases who underwent cutaneous punch biopsy from 2012 to 2019, 93% of the 283 biopsies were benign, 2 were probably benign and 18/283 (6.3%) yielded a malignant histopathology; 16/18 were from punch biopsy.

A clinical prediction rule to identify suspected breast cancer was prospectively developed on a cohort of Irish women referred for evaluation of breast symptoms, most commonly lump (50%) and mastalgia (33%). Independent clinical predictors were increasing age, presence of a lump, nipple discharge and nipple change, with the probability of breast cancer increasing with an increasing number of these variables.
The diagnostic strategy for work-up of a breast lump should not be modified for any risk factor other than age.
For women younger than 30 years, ultrasound is the initial imaging modality of choice. See .
For women 30 years and older, mammography or digital breast tomosynthesis diagnostic is the initial imaging modality of choice. See .
Simple cysts may undergo diagnostic aspiration.

The BI-RADS assessment category is used to determine further management. Category 0 – incomplete assessment; recall for additional imaging Category 1 – negative; continue routine screening. For women age 40 years or older, US is appropriate per ACR 2022. Category 2 - benign; continue routine screening. For women age 40 or older, US may be appropriate. Category 3 – probably benign; 6-month follow-up. For women age 40 or older with a palpable mass, category 3 diagnostic mammography and benign digital breast tomosynthesis diagnostic and US findings, additional imaging is not usually appropriate. Category 4 – suspicious, obtain US if not done; requires tissue diagnosis Category 5 - highly suggestive of malignancy, obtain US if not done; requires tissue diagnosis Category 6 – biopsy-proven malignancy; surgical excision when clinically appropriate
Negative imaging results should never overrule a strong clinical suspicion of breast cancer because up to 9% of breast cancers have negative imaging results.
